item.title: Introducing the United States Secretary of State (USSOS) Speech Dataset
item.description: arXiv:2610.19529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A large number of theories in international relations attribute importance to the rhetoric of leading foreign policy actors. Moreover, in recent years, there has been a significant growth in interest for producing machine-readable text of remarks from key foreign policy actors. Yet, researchers have, to date, focused primarily on the rhetoric of executive leaders and members of legislatures. To understand the construction of foreign policy in the public arena and dynamics in it, especially in the United States, we need a collection of fine-grained textual representation of the remarks of US Secretaries of State. An especially promising use for such a corpus of text is to measure attention areas in US foreign policy and its implication for the US's policies, including in foreign aid. In this note, We introduce the United States Secretary of State Dataset, a corpus of 17,700 remarks delivered by US Secretaries of State from 1997 to 2026. Using this dataset, we demonstrate that Secretaries of State frequently make public remarks, the likes of which can have substantively meaningful implications.
item.dc:creator: Benjanin Yoel, Jay Revolinsky

item.title: From Content Sharing to Opinion Shaping: A Theoretical Framework for Cascade-Driven Opinion Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.19867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online social networks (OSNs) tightly couple information diffusion and opinion formation, yet most existing models treat these processes separately. Building on the Friedkin-Johnsen on Cascades (FJC) model, which integrates opinion updating within stochastic information cascades, we advance its analytical characterization and systematic validation. We derive an exact conditional layer-wise recursion that reveals the statistical coupling between diffusion realizations and opinion evolution, showing that a closed-form recursion in unconditional expectations is not available. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a mean-field decoupling approximation (MFA) that yields a tractable linear recursion for the expected opinion trajectory. We also develop scalable tree-based reductions that drastically reduce computational complexity while preserving structural diffusion properties, and validate the analytical recursion and its approximations through extensive simulations. Using Stochastic Block Model networks with controlled initial opinion configurations, we show that, unlike the classical Friedkin-Johnsen model, which typically leads to global homogenization, the FJC dynamics generate richer regimes of bounded assimilation and sustained polarization. Overall, this work bridges diffusion and influence modeling, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding how cascade-driven interactions reshape collective opinion landscapes in structured social networks.
item.dc:creator: Elisabetta Biondi, Chiara Boldrini, Andrea Passarella, Marco Conti

item.title: Ergodic and Metastable Behavior of Stochastic Popularity Dynamics in Social Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.20021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies popularity dynamics in social networks, where users' engagement with competing channels is driven by intrinsic content quality, social influence, and popularity feedback. We introduce a stochastic model in which users interact through a directed influence network and channel exposure depends jointly on these three mechanisms. We first characterize the resulting dynamics in the absence of intrinsic quality, showing that popularity concentrates asymptotically on a single channel, leading to a winner-takes-all regime. When all channels have positive intrinsic quality, we establish ergodicity of the popularity process and characterize its long-run behavior. We further show that, when intrinsic quality is small, the system exhibits metastable behavior: it can remain for long periods near configurations dominated by a single channel before transitioning to another. These results highlight how weak quality differences can coexist with strong path dependence induced by popularity feedback. We then investigate platform-level interventions and propose controls that compensate for network-induced exposure biases and mitigate excessive concentration. Analytical results are illustrated through numerical simulations and an empirical analysis of YouTube data, whose observed popularity dynamics are consistent with the proposed stochastic framework. The results provide a mathematical framework for understanding the interplay between quality, social influence, and reinforcement in online popularity dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Chiara Ravazzi, Paolo Frasca, Gaya Cocca

item.title: Uncovering higher-order interactions from memory in observed dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.20095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many complex systems involve group interactions, which can readily be represented by higher-order structures such as hypergraphs. However, when observing a system's dynamical evolution, establishing whether that evolution actually results from higher-order interactions, or whether pairwise interactions suffice to explain the data, remains a challenge. Even in the simple case of a temporal sequence of nodes visited during a diffusion process, such a task is intricate. Indeed, group interactions leave their traces as memory on the observed nodes, while path dependence in a purely pairwise process can mimic that same footprint without any group structure. To resolve this, we propose an inference pipeline based on a hidden Markov model (HMM) that tests, directly from an observed sequence of nodes carrying no group labels, whether higher-order interactions are required to describe the dynamics. The HMM latent states represent higher-order interactions, seen as hyperedges of an unobserved hypergraph, so that their detection becomes a model selection problem between the HMM class and a class of null models without higher-order interactions. We first validate this approach on synthetic node sequences generated from random walks on graphs and hypergraphs, showing that it recovers both the number and the composition of the underlying hyperedges, while correctly rejecting them when the generating process is pairwise. As a second step, we consider a validation based on empirical data, namely empirical trajectories of ball possession in football matches. This application shows that the pipeline goes beyond providing statistical evidence of the presence of higher-order interactions, and yields interpretable underlying structures: the recovered hyperedges map directly onto recognizable tactical team formations.
item.dc:creator: Arthur Rondeau, Alain Barrat, Roland Bouffanais

item.title: Contagious Misinterpretations: Social Learning with Shared Interpretations
item.description: arXiv:2610.20381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When people discuss which of several hypotheses is true, they share not only their beliefs but also their interpretation of each one, that is, the distribution of signals each hypothesis is expected to produce. This interpretation is an opinion about what each hypothesis means and what evidence it predicts, and it is revised only through conversation, not by confronting it with the observed data. Standard non-Bayesian social learning captures only belief-sharing and keeps the likelihoods private. We study what happens when agents share both beliefs and likelihoods under static networks. We show that interpretations converge geometrically to a common reading shaped by the most influential agents. Then, beliefs concentrate, almost surely and at an exponential rate, on the hypothesis that, under this consensus interpretation, best explains the signals privately observed by all agents taken together. As a result, sharing interpretations can lead a population to adopt, unanimously and confidently, a hypothesis it would have rejected if it had shared only beliefs. Whether this helps or hurts when a true hypothesis exists depends on how accurately agents initially read the data they observe. When every agent initially interprets the true hypothesis exactly as the data it would observe, sharing interpretations cannot strictly improve learning and can strictly harm it when agents observe different data distributions. When interpretations are logically coherent and some agents misread their own data, sharing can either rescue the population, leading it to learn the true hypothesis, if an accurate reading dominates the interpretation network, or corrupt it, leading it to a wrong hypothesis, if a misreading one does.
item.dc:creator: Pol Rodr\'iguez Farr\'es, Jesus Cerquides

item.title: Popularity Trajectories and Mixing Patterns of Urban Venues in Two European Cities
item.description: arXiv:2610.18917v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Urban venues such as restaurants, shops, bars and parks host the daily life of a city, and their collective rise and fall signals how vibrant a neighbourhood is. The usual assumption is that a venue's fortunes follow its neighbourhood's, so that how wealthy an area is and how many people live there will decide a venue's performance. Yet whether there is a common performance trajectory shared by venues over time is underexplored. In this study, we use 5.5 years of Foursquare data for about 10^4 venues in London and Barcelona. We found six distinguishable shapes recur in both cities, that are (1) Fall, (2) Rise, (3) Rise & Fall, (4) Steady, (5) Ephemeral (an early hit that loses popularity fast) and (6) Underdogs (a slow starter that gains popularity late). However, no recovery shape appears, that is neither city yields a U-shaped fall-and-rise group. Additionally, we found that deprivation and population density are not indicative which shape a venue follows. We also discovered that how early a shape can be recognized depends on when its distinctive segment occurs, not a shape's complexity. Proximity between venues, however, does predict how well-performing a venue is. We uncovered a mixing pattern where venues of the same shape tend to locate together more often than chance within roughly 200 to 600 metres. Finally, our qualitative reading of two contrasting districts, one rising in London and one falling in Barcelona, show that comparable socioeconomic conditions but divergent gentrification histories can generate vastly different popularity trajectories. All in all, our results altogether point at that urban vibrancy emerges at the block- and street- level, and social and historical contexts matter in terms of the characteristics of such patterns.
item.dc:creator: Wang Ngai Yeung, Lakmal Meegahapola, Daniele Quercia, Riccardo Di Clemente

item.title: Structural Dependence, Imitation or Herding? A Multi-Agent Simulation of Global Intermedia Agenda Setting
item.description: arXiv:2610.20144v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: News outlets in poorer countries cover the world much as the leading outlets of rich countries do. Two explanations compete. One says they depend on Western news agencies for lack of resources. The other says they choose to copy prestigious outlets or whoever moves first. Observation cannot tell these apart. This study measured how closely 18 national outlets in Bangladesh, Kenya, South Africa, India, Malaysia and Nigeria followed four core outlets in how much attention they gave, which angle they took and when they published, on the wars in Ukraine and Gaza and two UN climate conferences in 2022-2024. It then ran a simulation in which language models acted as the outlets' editors and dependence, imitation and herding were switched on and off. Of nine tests, one held: outlets that relied more on wire copy published sooner after the core did. Tier and local stake showed no effect distinguishable from none. The herding test was supported and the imitation test was not. The simulation did not decide between the mechanisms, because the dependence rule, as fitted, reduced to publishing wire copy. Wire copy sets the clock of the periphery's foreign news. Whether it sets the agenda stays open.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Yousuf, Arif Md Tareque Habib

item.title: What Makes a Social Agent's Interactions Effective? Learning from Verifiable Outcomes in Paired Worlds
item.description: arXiv:2610.20195v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Effective social interaction requires more than fluent responses: agents must reach plans that fit the participants' needs and circumstances. Existing evaluations of social agents mainly rely on LLM judges that rate the conversation, without checking the resulting plan. We introduce HICO-Bench, a benchmark of 180 everyday coordination scenarios, such as resource allocation, scheduling, and authorization, in which two agents with private information converse and then independently record the plan they agreed on. A program checks Feasibility (the two records match and satisfy both participants' private conditions), and an LLM judge checks Integrity (the conversation supports the recorded plan); passing both is a Verified Success. Each scenario has two versions that share the same public context but differ in one private condition, so the correct plan differs between them. Across thirteen LLMs, 36% of conversations rated highly for goal completion fail Verified Success. To learn from outcomes that arrive only at the end of a conversation, we propose Paired-Credit Policy Optimization (PaCPO). After each turn, PaCPO asks the agent for a tentative plan, checks it in both versions of the scenario, and rewards the turns after which the tentative plans fit their respective versions. PaCPO raises Qwen3-8B's Verified Success from 20.4% to 28.3%.
item.dc:creator: Caixin Kang, Ke Wang, Yuchuan Wu, Xiaoqiang Wang, Ling Li, Bingxue Qiu, Yongbin Li, Yoichi Sato

item.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2610.20548v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.
item.dc:creator: Ali Zamani, Soroush Esfahanian, Erfan Shahabi, Mohammad Taher Pilehvar, Azadeh Shakery, Yadollah Yaghoobzadeh

item.title: Semantic Communities and Boundary-Spanning Lyrics in K-pop: A Graph-Based Unsupervised Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2602.12881v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We examine how lyric representation shapes computational similarity using four 384-dimensional multilingual MiniLM representations of 7,891 K-pop songs by 1,456 artists from charts spanning 2000 to October 2023. Whole-song truncated embeddings provide the strongest standardized separation between neighbouring and random song pairs (1.995), compared with 1.931 for chunked documents, although chunked representations show greater adjusted Rand agreement and line-based representations yield higher modularity. Using whole-song embeddings, we construct a weighted cosine nearest-neighbour graph ($k=30$). A representative Louvain partition identifies 21 operational communities, without a corresponding robust plateau in the Markov Stability analysis. AI-assisted examination of selected lyrics and terms suggests overlapping patterns of memory, separation, longing, self-reflection, attraction, and performance. Community membership is associated with character-script composition (Cram\'er's $V=0.294$; permutation $p=0.001$). High-participation songs exhibit broader cross-community connectivity, while participation has weak negative associations with embedding-relative novelty. These findings show how representation choices and textual characteristics influence the network organization of a cultural corpus, subject to limitations from truncation, graph construction, and the absence of independent human semantic validation.
item.dc:creator: Oktay Karaku\c{s}, Can Ey\"upo\u{g}lu

item.title: Coupling Macro Dynamics and Micro States for Long-Horizon Social Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2604.05516v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Social network simulation aims to model collective opinion dynamics in large populations, but existing LLM-based simulators mainly focus on aggregate dynamics while largely ignoring individual internal states. This limits their ability to capture opinion reversals driven by gradual individual shifts and makes them unreliable in long-horizon simulations. We propose MF-MDP, a social simulation framework that tightly couples macro-level collective dynamics with micro-level individual states. MF-MDP explicitly models per-agent latent opinion states with a state transition mechanism, combining individual Markov Decision Processes at the micro level with a mean-field collective framework at the macro level. This allows individual behaviors to change internal states gradually rather than trigger instant reactions, enabling the simulator to distinguish agents that are close to switching from those that are far from switching, capture opinion reversals, and maintain accuracy over long horizons. Across real-world events, MF-MDP supports stable simulation of long-horizon social processes with up to 40,000 interactions, compared with about 300 in the baseline MF-LLM, while reducing long-horizon KL divergence by 75.3% (1.2490 to 0.3089) and reversal KL by 66.9% (1.6425 to 0.5434), significantly mitigating the drift observed in MF-LLM. Code is available at ai4ss.github.io/M2Sim.
item.dc:creator: Yunyao Zhang, Yihao Ai, Zuocheng Ying, Qirui Mi, Junqing Yu, Wei Yang, Zikai Song

item.title: DeTox-Fed: Detecting Toxic Conversations in the Fediverse with Federated Graph Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2605.21054v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rise of decentralized social networks (DSNs), and in particular the rapid uptake of the Fediverse (e.g., Pleroma, Mastodon, Lemmygrad), introduces new challenges in content moderation. Independent instances host their own data, follow different moderation policies, and often observe only partial views of conversations. We present DeTox-Fed, a federated graph-learning framework for detecting toxic conversations in DSNs without requiring instances to share raw conversations or moderation labels. Each instance constructs a local conversation graph, where nodes represent conversation trees and edges capture shared user participation across conversations. A Graph Neural Network is then trained in a federated learning setup, allowing instances to collaboratively learn a toxicity classifier while preserving data locality. Unlike text-only moderation approaches, DeTox-Fed combines conversational structure, user-interaction patterns, conversation-level statistics, and aggregate sentiment signals. We evaluate the framework on a large Pleroma conversation dataset and a second one from Mastodon, showing that it achieves stable toxic conversation detection under limited local labels, partial client participation, and varying moderation thresholds. Our results indicate that federated graph-based moderation is a promising direction for semi-automated moderation in decentralized social networks.
item.dc:creator: Pantelitsa Leonidou, Nikos Salamanos, Sotiris Gypsiotis, Michael Sirivianos

item.title: When Can Digital Personas Reliably Approximate Human Survey Findings?
item.description: arXiv:2605.10659v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Digital personas powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human survey respondents, yet it remains unclear when they can reliably approximate human survey findings. We answer this question using the LISS panel, constructing personas from respondents' background variables and pre-2023 survey histories, then testing them against the same respondents' held-out post-cutoff answers. Across four persona architectures, three LLMs, and two prediction tasks, we assess performance at the question, respondent, distributional, equity, and clustering levels. Digital personas improve alignment with human response distributions, especially in domains tied to stable attributes and values, but remain limited for individual prediction and fail to recover multivariate respondent structure. Retrieval-augmented architectures provide the clearest gains, but performance depends more on human response structure than on model choice: personas perform best for low-variability questions and common respondent patterns, and worst for subjective, heterogeneous, or rare responses. Our results provide practical guidance on when digital personas could be appropriate for survey research and when human validation remains necessary.
item.dc:creator: Mumin Jia, Yilin Chen, Divya Sharma, Jairo Diaz-Rodriguez

item.title: Blackknife: Query-Free Black-Box Rewiring Attacks on Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.29240v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) perform well on graphs with multiple node and relation types, but their robustness to attacks with restricted structural access remains insufficiently understood. We propose Blackknife, a query-free, strict black-box evasion attack that observes only the one-hop structures of the attacked nodes, their ground-truth labels, and raw features within the permitted action space. No victim-model outputs are used to train the surrogate, generate perturbations, or select attacks.Blackknife trains a shared surrogate using only observable edges and relation types, then optimizes structural perturbations through continuous relaxation and projected gradient ascent. Each rewiring operation deletes one edge and adds another of the same relation type, preserving the target node's total degree and degree for each relation type. A cosine-similarity penalty and an adaptive structural classifier further regularize the perturbations through bilevel optimization. Experiments on different datasets demonstrate competitive attack success rates across five victim architectures and three defense settings. The results expose HGNN vulnerabilities under jointly restricted graph access and query-free attack generation.
item.dc:creator: Honglin Gao, Junhao Ren, Lan Zhao, Yue Yang, Peilin Du, Jindong Chang, Gaoxi Xiao

item.title: Filling holes in science draws collective attention, but most higher-order holes remain unexplored
item.description: arXiv:2608.28822v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most scientific discoveries justify their significance by filling holes between existing ideas and arguments. Representing knowledge as high-dimensional concept embeddings, we use persistent homology to detect scientific holes of increasing order, from lower-order gaps between disconnected ideas to higher-order cavities within unevenly connected ones; then we identify the research that fills them. Researchers who close holes draw outsized collective attention, staging novelty that the citing literature rewards, most strongly in discovery-oriented fields and least in design-oriented fields. Closing a hole is followed by persistent work on the same combinations of concepts at many times the rate of comparable holes left open. Yet as knowledge grows, higher-order holes explode while the fraction of research that fills them collapses, leaving most higher-order combinations unexplored. These results call for a richer science of holes and mark a frontier where contemporary AI might help fill the gaps human science opens.
item.dc:creator: Jiajie Luo, James A. Evans
